The Arboreal salamander (Aneides lugubris) exhibits a relatively slow life history compared to many other plethodontids of similar body size. Females deposit their clutches in natural cavities within decaying oak or madrone logs, where the developing embryos are guarded until hatching. After an incubation period that lasts approximately 107 days [ab = approximately 107 days] when temperatures average 13 °C [T = 13 °C], the neonates emerge at a wet weight of just 0.0335 grams [Wwb = 0.0335 grams]. This remarkably small birth mass, reflecting a larval stage that is completed entirely within the egg, contrasts sharply with the adult dimensions these animals eventually attain. Field surveys of populations in the coastal redwood forests of California indicate that adult females, following years of growth, reach a maximum body mass of 22.6 grams [Wwi = 22.6 grams], a value that corresponds to the asymptotic size described for this species. The dramatic ontogenetic shift from a 0.0335 gram neonate to a 22.6 gram reproductively active female underscores the considerable energetic investment required to reach maturity in this slow-growing taxon.

Metabolic investigations under controlled laboratory conditions have provided insights into the energetic demands of this sedentary amphibian. When kept at a stable temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], individuals exhibit a maximum basal metabolic rate of 0.0024 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 0.0024 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This extraordinarily low oxygen consumption value is consistent with the species' secretive, fossorial habits and its reliance on low-energy prey items such as beetles and ants. In comparison to sympatric, more active plethodontids, this resting metabolic rate reflects a physiological strategy tuned to the cool, humid microclimates of the species' preferred arboreal refugia. The measurements were obtained from post-absorptive animals during their inactive diurnal period, ensuring that the data represented true basal conditions. Such a low metabolic overhead may allow individuals to persist on limited foraging opportunities during prolonged dry spells, a common ecological constraint in California's Mediterranean climate zones, but it also places strict limits on the pace of growth and reproduction.

The onset of reproductive capability in this species occurs following a substantial period of post-metamorphic growth. Females attain sexual maturity only after approximately 3 years following metamorphosis [tp = approximately 3 years following metamorphosis] when maintained at a thermal regime averaging 23 °C [T = 23 °C]. This three-year delay before the first vitellogenic cycle commences is among the longest recorded for any North American plethodontid, reflecting the species' K-selected life history strategy. During this lengthy juvenile period, individuals must accumulate sufficient lipid reserves to support both the metabolic costs of activity and the eventual production of a clutch. The developmental trajectory from a recently metamorphosed juvenile, which typically leaves the nest site at approximately 3 months after hatching  at 23 °C [T = 23 °C], through to the attainment of full adult body mass, represents a gradual and energetically conservative process. This slow maturation is likely an adaptation to the unpredictable and often scarce food resources available in the epiphytic microhabitats these salamanders occupy.

Reproductive output is modest, consistent with the species' prolonged developmental schedule. Breeding females produce a single clutch of approximately 20 eggs [N_R_i = single clutch of approximately 20 eggs] each season, yielding a maximum annual reproductive rate of one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year]. This low fecundity is a classic correlate of extended parental care, as females are known to coil around their egg masses to protect them from desiccation and fungal infection throughout the incubation period. The trade-off between offspring number and per-offspring investment is evident here: the large, nutrient-rich eggs enable the production of fully-formed, terrestrial hatchlings that bypass a free-living aquatic larval stage. Given that many females may skip reproduction entirely in particularly dry years, the effective lifetime reproductive output is likely substantially lower than the theoretical maximum. Coupled with the long maturation time, this slow reproductive tempo makes the species particularly vulnerable to habitat disturbance. Furthermore, the maximum documented lifespan under natural conditions extends to 4,015 days [am = 4,015 days] at 23 °C [T = 23 °C], a longevity that allows for multiple, if infrequent, reproductive opportunities across an individual's lifetime.

The prolonged life span of approximately 11 years [am = approximately 11 years] stands in marked contrast to the rapid life cycles of many low-elevation amphibians, a disparity that highlights the role of environmental predictability in shaping senes at a temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C]cence patterns. The relatively cool and stable temperatures within the deep crevices of old-growth trees may reduce oxidative stress and slow the physiological aging process. A comparable longevity has been documented in other arboreal plethodontids from the Pacific Northwest, suggesting a convergent life-history syndrome associated with the retention of ancestral terrestrial habits. The species is long-lived enough that individual females may encounter multiple favorable breeding seasons over their reproductive tenure, offsetting the low fecundity per event. This demographic buffering is essential for population persistence in an environment where recruitment events are sporadic and highly contingent upon autumn and winter precipitation. Adult survivorship, therefore, acts as the primary demographic rate governing population stability, making the preservation of mature forest habitat with abundant microrefugia critical for the long-term conservation of Aneides lugubris across its fragmented range.
